extracted.intended_audience: general readers and writers of short stories / literary fiction (early-20th-century tone)
extracted.subtask_description: Guiding/recognizable aesthetic and compositional features for a collection of short romantic tales and 'half-told' stories anchored by a unifying theme of mystery (early 20th-century literary style).

rubrics_metrics.name: Thread / unifying theme (the unknown quantity)
rubrics_metrics.description: The thread that binds the stories in this book is ... the sign of the unknown quantity, the sense of mystery and strangeness, that runs through human life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a recurring, sometimes subtle central idea (here: the 'unknown quantity' — mystery in human life) to give cohesion to a set of otherwise diverse tales. The unifying thread need not be plot-linked; it can be thematic or tonal, recurring in different guises across stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety within unity (stories as distinct 'lakes')
rubrics_metrics.description: Each of these hidden lakes has its own character and therefore its own charm ... They are so unlike. But the same stream ... runs through them all, and lives in them all, and makes them all belong together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow individual stories to have distinct characters, moods, lengths, and settings while maintaining a connecting element (theme, motif, narrator voice) so the collection feels varied yet coherent. Emphasize individual character of each piece rather than forcing uniformity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Half-Told Tales: suggestiveness and brevity
rubrics_metrics.description: Between the longer stories there are three groups of tales that are told in a briefer and different manner. They are like etchings in which more is suggested than is in the picture. For this reason they are called Half-Told Tales, in the hope that they may mean to the reader more than they say.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concision, implication, and strategic omission to create stories that gesture beyond their words; favour suggestion over exhaustive explanation. Short pieces can be deliberately incomplete to invite reader interpretation and resonance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story origins: grow from slight hints / local legends
rubrics_metrics.description: Four of the stories have grown out of slight hints, for which I return thanks. For the two Breton legends ... I am indebted to my friend ... and for an incident which suggested 'The Night Call' ... and for the germ of 'The Mansion', to my friend ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be open to small hints, folk legends, or overheard incidents as seeds for fiction. A brief anecdote or traditional tale can be transformed into a full story by imaginative expansion while acknowledging source material where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on human, everyday mystery (not occult sensationalism)
rubrics_metrics.description: I am not thinking now of the so-called 'realm of the occult' ... I am thinking of much more human and familiar things, quite natural and inevitable as it seems, which make us feel that life is threaded through and through by the unknown quantity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize ordinary human experiences that retain an element of inexplicability—the subtle, moral, and psychological surprises of life—rather than relying on supernatural spectacle. Let wonder and mystery emerge from character and circumstance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone / moral attitude: hopeful interpretation of mystery
rubrics_metrics.description: Without the unknown quantity life would be easier, perhaps, but certainly less interesting. ... we can live with it and work with it bravely, hopefully, happily, if we believe that after all it means good--infinite good, passing comprehension--to all who live in love.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt an overall tone that treats mystery as meaningful or ultimately benevolent; even sorrowful events can lead to a 'happy' resolution or moral consolation. The authorial voice may guide readers toward an emotionally affirmative reading of ambiguous events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of vivid character portraiture and concrete detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Toinette was ... just a pretty French Canadian girl with an oval face, brown hair, and eyes like a very dark topaz. Her voice was rich and vibrant, like the middle notes of a 'cello, but she spoke a dialect that was as rustic as a cabbage. Her hands were small, but rather red and rough.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Render characters through concrete, sensory details (physical traits, voice comparisons, dialect, habits) to create immediacy and individuality. Juxtapose idealizing statements (e.g., 'genius for loving') with earthy specifics to deepen realism and sympathy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of local color / strong sense of place
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a chain of little lakes ... lying in the forest that clothes the blue Laurentian Mountains in the Province of Quebec ... The lighthouse on the Isle of the Wise Virgin ... still looks out over the blue waters of the Gulf of Saint Lawrence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anchor stories in distinctive landscapes, regional details, and cultural touchstones (e.g., Breton folk beliefs, Quebec settings) to give atmosphere and to feed plot and theme. Settings can function symbolically (the lakes as characters) as well as scenically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narratorial commentary: occasional explicit moralizing or explanatory voice
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not common, nor regular, nor altogether justifiable by precept and authority. Reason is against it; and the doctors of the church have always spoken severely ... But the fact remains ... There is still something around us and within that baffles and surprises us.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow the narrator to step in with reflections, moral judgments, or generalizations to frame episodes and to point readers toward thematic concerns. This commentator voice can lend wisdom, ironies, or pastoral warmth compatible with early-20th-century fiction.
